questionText: A circle has a radius of 21 cm. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7)
A circle has a radius of 35 cm. What is its circumference? (Use π = 22/7)
A circle is a set of all points that are equidistant from a fixed point called the:
hints: All points on a circle are the same distance from one special point.
This fixed point in the middle is called the centre.
The centre is NOT on the circle — it's inside it!

stepByStep.text: A circle is defined by its centre and radius.
stepByStep.latex: \text{All points at distance } r \text{ from centre}

stepByStep.text: The fixed point is the centre.

misconceptions.A: Radius is the DISTANCE from centre to circle, not the point itself
misconceptions.B: Diameter is a line segment, not a point
misconceptions.D: Chord is a line segment with endpoints on the circle

questionText: If the radius of a circle is 9.5 cm, what is its diameter?
hints: The diameter is always twice the radius.
= 19 cm

misconceptions.A: Divided by 2 instead of multiplying (found radius from diameter)
misconceptions.D: Diameter is NOT the same as radius — it's twice the radius

questionText: The longest chord of a circle is called the:
hints: A chord is a line segment with both endpoints on the circle.
The longest possible chord passes through the centre.
A chord through the centre = diameter. It's the longest chord.

stepByStep.text: A chord through the centre is the longest chord possible.

misconceptions.A: Radius goes from centre to the circle — it's not a chord (both ends must be ON the circle)
misconceptions.B: Arc is a curved part of the circle, not a straight line segment
misconceptions.D: Circumference is the distance AROUND the circle, not a chord

questionText: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?
hints: Every diameter divides the circle into two equal halves.
How many diameters can you draw? You can draw one in ANY direction!
Infinite diameters = infinite axes of symmetry.

stepByStep.text: Every diameter is an axis of symmetry.

misconceptions.C: A circle has MORE symmetry than any polygon, not less

questionText: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 21 cm. (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Circumference = 2 × π × r = 2 × 22/7 × 21.
Simplify: 21 ÷ 7 = 3. So C = 2 × 22 × 3.

misconceptions.A: 66 = πr (forgot to multiply by 2, or used πd with r instead of d)

questionText: A circle has a radius of 35 cm. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7)

Find the area of a circle with radius 7 cm. (Use π = 22/7)
hints: One 7 cancels: 22/7 × 7 = 22. Then 22 × 7 = 154.
Area = 154 cm².

misconceptions.C: 22 = 22/7 × 7 (only multiplied by r once, not r²)

questionText: Find the area of a circle with diameter 14 cm. (Use π = 22/7)
hints: First find radius: r = d/2 = 14/2 = 7 cm.
Area = πr² = 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 cm².
Same as the previous problem! Diameter 14 → radius 7 → area 154.

misconceptions.B: 616 = π × 14² (used diameter instead of radius in area formula!)

questionText: A circular track has radius 35 m. How far does a runner go in 3 laps? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: 1 lap = circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 35.

questionText: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. What is its area? (Use π = 22/7)
A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. Each part is called a:
hints: 'Semi' means half. So semicircle = half circle.
A diameter passes through the centre and divides the circle into exactly 2 equal halves.
Each half = a semicircle.

stepByStep.text: Diameter splits circle into 2 equal halves.

misconceptions.C: Arc is any curved portion of a circle, not specifically half
misconceptions.D: Sector is a 'pizza slice' shape (bounded by 2 radii and an arc)

questionText: A wheel has diameter 28 cm. How many complete rotations will it make to cover 440 cm? (Use π = 22/7)
hints: 1 rotation = 1 circumference = πd = 22/7 × 28.
28 ÷ 7 = 4. C = 22 × 4 = 88 cm per rotation.
Rotations = 440 ÷ 88 = 5.

misconceptions.D: 88 is the circumference, not the number of rotations

questionText: Circles that have the same centre but different radii are called:
hints: 'Con-centric' means 'with the same centre.'
Like rings on a target board — same centre, different sizes.
These are concentric circles.

stepByStep.text: Same centre + different radii = concentric circles.

misconceptions.A: Congruent circles have EQUAL radii (same size), not same centre
misconceptions.C: Equal circles = congruent circles (same size, maybe different centres)
misconceptions.D: Tangent circles touch at exactly one point

questionText: The area of a circle is 616 cm². Find its radius. (Use π = 22/7)

misconceptions.A: 7 is the radius for area = 154, not 616
misconceptions.D: 196 = r², not r (forgot to take square root)

questionText: For a circle with radius 7 cm, which is larger numerically: the circumference or the area?
hints: Numerically: 154 > 44.
The area (154) is larger than the circumference (44). But note: they have different units!

misconceptions.D: While they have different units, we CAN compare numerically

questionText: How many radii and diameters can a circle have?
hints: A radius can go from the centre to ANY point on the circle. How many points are on a circle?
Infinite points → infinite radii. And since every diameter passes through the centre in any direction...
Infinite diameters too! Both are infinite.

stepByStep.text: Infinite points on circle → infinite radii
Infinite directions through centre → infinite diameters

misconceptions.A: A circle has many more than just 1 of each
misconceptions.D: Diameters are also infinite, not just 2

questionText: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with diameter 14 cm. (Use π = 22/7)
hints: Perimeter of a semicircle = half the circumference + the diameter (the straight edge).
Half circumference = πd/2 = 22/7 × 14/2 = 22/7 × 7 = 22 cm.
Perimeter = 22 + 14 = 36 cm.

misconceptions.A: 22 is only the curved part (forgot the straight diameter edge)
misconceptions.C: 44 = full circumference (that's the full circle, not semicircle)
misconceptions.D: May have added 44+14=58 (used full circumference + diameter)
